Thomas_Link:

“My guess is that the “default matrix” is causing interference. … The TIFF was created using the standard matrix, and I can’t just select “none” or something like that in the input profile.”

That matrix, or any replacement you choose has to be in the processing pipeline if you want your rendition to look presentable. It represents what I’ll colloquially call the “camera color space”, it describes the color space of that particular camera for transforms to other color spaces, ultimately the color space of the rendition medium. Just setting it to Rec2020 or some other arbitrary color space bolloxes the whole transformation chain.

Okay, here’s a test of that specific replacement. I opened a raw with some color in rawproc, my hack raw processor. First screenshot is the rendition to display using the appropriate ‘standard matrix’ for my Nikon D7000:

Camera_standard_matrix800×515 452 KB

If you look at the toolchain pane in the top-left of the program window, you’ll see a ‘colorspace:assign’ operator, that’s where my program associates the camera profile with the image. In the parameter pane at the bottom-left, note that the option “assign camera profile” at the bottom is selected, those 9 numbers are the camera matrix for my Nikon D7000. Note that the “profile file” option at the top is not selected, but has a Rec2020 profile file in the box. Let’s select that option, and regard the difference:

Rec2020_matrix800×515 445 KB

The matrix for a camera, either embedded in the sofware or supplied in a separate profile file, is purpose-built for the specific spectral response of that camera. Unless you want to just do goofy stuff, you need that as a starting point.

does ART also use the scene referred workflow?

Similarly, I’m not sure what “scene-referred” actually refers to in darktable. My guess is that, in the past, darktable processed everything in a display color space (sRGB or some other gamma- or tone-curved space). But at some point, that was changed so that it uses a linear working space until all the processing is done, and then the picture is converted to a gamma-curved color space for display (somebody please correct me if that’s the wrong impression).

ART uses a similar flow – a linear working space that is converted to a display color space at the end. Not all of the tools operate linearly, though, or even in the working space. Some things are better done in a nonlinear, sometimes non-RGB, space (the DT tools probably do this, too, but I have no first-hand knowledge).

Do you think ART is better than DT especially with respect to a proper mathematical approach?

I started out using darktable 6 or 7 years ago, switched to RawTherapee, then to ART. I found that I could get better results with less work using ART; other folks probably have the opposite experience. For making profiles, ART and RawTherapee have a button that exports a reference TIFF file using a process configured for making camera profiles (you still have to prepare the image, as usual). There are many ways to crunch the numbers; I’m not sure there is a single approach that’s always better.

@ Thomas_Link, I’ve downloaded your raw file and will take a look at it. I’m not familiar with the SpyderChecker target, so I’ll need to play around with that for a while.

Here are a few suggestions about the setup:

  • The surround should be as dark as possible to reduce flare effects and minimize extraneous colors leaking into the frame. I use an old dark cloth from my large format days, and spread it out to cover as much area as possible. Also, remove all the shiny objects for the same reason (specular reflections are very bright, like having several tiny suns in the frame). A lens hood can also be beneficial.

  • Reposition the target or camera a little to reduce the glare in the upper right corner. If the color patches have a bit of a glare on them, they will photograph lighter and less colorful than they should.

  • The photo looks as though it may have been taken in the shade. That’s OK if you are making a profile to be used for pictures taken in the shade, but making a daylight profile (direct sun + blue sky) should be more generally applicable.

  • I’ll also suggest stopping the lens down a little bit more, to the f/5.6 - f/8 range, to minimize any aberrations.

@Thomas_Link : Have you calibrated and profiled your monitor already? I think that’s the more important step if you want reliable color rendering:

  • there’s a lot of variation between monitors, so if your monitor isn’t set up correctly, you don’t know what you are looking at
  • as there is a lot of variation between monitors, what you see is not what most others will see. If your monitor is calibrated and profiled, you’ll at least make sure that what you sent out has the colours you expect.

As you notice, profiling the camera is a lot of work. And getting a proper profile does not in itself guarantee correct colours, you also need to control or measure the illuminant for the images on which you use that profile (normally, such profiles are valid for one illuminant only…)
